commentBody: Nice theme, and a fun, fast solve. Thanks!

Note to Caitlin: 

Daniel TIGER was originally a character on a more famous show:  Mr. Rogers' Neighborhood.

You've probably heard of that one.

Not to brag, but the cloud of periwinkle blue in my fall garden right now shows that I have real
ASTER MASTERY.

Well, I gave it a shot. But the paper cut apercus were so so funny!  Can’t you just see someone calmly reciting one of those instead of hopping around swearing?
I found the themers truly delightful, and they are, to be sure, in a crossword, but I found little, if anything, puzzling here; I was just filling in a lot of entries on autopilot.

So if ever there was an example of a puzzle geared more for the constructor than the solver, this is it. That’s ok, I still had fun seeing these clever theme entries and would love to hear more about how he came up with them (I’m assuming a computer algorithm, and that’s ok too, they were really very entertaining!) The problem with the solve is, once you get the theme (which is right away), then figuring out the themers becomes exceedingly easy because half the letters are duplicated. So if ever there was a Sunday puzzle which begged and deserved for more challenging clues around the themes, this was it, and unfortunately those were very straightforward. I did love the clues for POINTLESS and UNCORK. I like the idea of PETPASSPORT but I can tell you that having traveled with my furry friend on many occasions no airline calls it that. Still it’s a great entry. Speaking of constructor centered puzzles, here’s mine, admittedly and with full disclosure. This puzzle has been rattling around in my closet for a long time. It is my Everest, the one I made just to see if I could. I'm not sure how fair or enjoyable it will be, but I decided its time had come. Frequent NYT solvers will understand why after they solve it. I'm curious to hear what you all think about it. (I’ve already gotten some fair negative feedback, but some positive as well, so YMMV). https://crosshare.org/crosswords/Qj4H3BgDSddtUECbw1OW/out-of-the-box
14 years, fastest Sunday ever. A bit like a word-find, no?
Daniel Tiger has been around since 1954... definitely skews older, not younger.
Fun puzzle, but I solve digitally and somehow thought I was going to get a bunch of little hearts pulsating or one big one when I finished.
Fast solve, but the theme was delightful.

Cluing Diwali or Holi as a "Hindi shindig" is the cultural equivalent of calling Christmas an "English extravaganza."
Hindi is a language, not a religion. These holidays are celebrated globally by over a billion people speaking dozens of other languages, just like Christmas is celebrated by people speaking dozens of languages.
Breezy puzzle with a cute theme.  Worth it for HINDISHINDIG alone.  LOTSA fun but over too soon

Fast, fun. For future puzzle possibilities, in Russia, if you’re travelling outside the country with a musical instrument you might be asked to get the instrument its own passport. I learned this from a friend.
What is the meaning of papercutapercu? Is it simply the p and t are cut?
Who else, like me, confidently slapped in TILT for [Be inclined]?

Always love me a Michael Lieberman puzzle, even if I did spend the last couple of minutes parsing the _EY / _ANHMI/Y cross. Never heard of Queen Bey (yes, I looked it up after solving; still never heard the nickname), never had a BANH MI—and FLEUR-DE-LIS can also be spelled FLEUR-DE-LYS. Fair, but tough for me. 

One nit: Holi and Diwali are Hindu, not Hindi, festivals. Celebrants are apt to be Hindu, but may or may not speak Hindi. Even in service of a theme, HINDI SHINDIG is really a stretch.
Please explain the shaded squares like I'm 5. Thank you.
I'm going to apologize in advance -- I had a post which I've tried to get in three times with no result, so they will all probably show up tomorrow.  Forgive me for cluttering up the comments!

For anyone who got a kick out of the Roadrunner puzzle last year, you should check out the movie “Coyote vs Acme”. I just saw it, it was so much fun, heartwarming, nostalgic, and a real hoot (or meep, or beep). And for the record they sprinkled a few meeps in with the beeps for the sake of world peace, but it put to rest, once and for all, that the Roadrunner’s name, and the transliteration of his speech, is indeed “Beep Beep”. Also there was a call out coincidentally to yesterday’s Sisyphus reference.

Cute theme. One minor grouse- calling Diwali and Holi Hindi festivals instead of Hindu festivals is a bit like calling Hanukkah a Hebrew festival or Eid an Arabic festival. And while one could argue the festivals are called that in the Hindi language, it's a bit of a stretch since the origins of the words are from Sanskrit and they are called by these names in a few other languages as well. Other than that, was a fantastic Sunday puzzle.

Um, so yeah, that felt more like an exercise at the department of motor vehicles, than completing a crossword puzzle. Just filling in all the necessary boxes without thinking too much. 

Clever idea, but man, on the ez side.

I, for one, did not see the theme right away. I was bopping around the entire puzzle filling in what I could and puzzling out the rest. I did get the theme answers as I went along, but never looked at what might be going on with them until the end. And to be honest, was a little underwhelmed when I figured it out. Fun fact, October 9 was VERDI's Birthday. And today's opera broadcast was La Traviata, which I can't OVERDo listening to, Rigoletto, not so much. However, my earworm today comes from the Marvel Cinematic Universe, cast members of the various movies dancing to RASPUTIN. https://youtu.be/HPt-jGUHNzE?si=aMVD1U5rFx4S5tCL
DNF. The intersection of wibbly wobbly and newts did me in.
I loved this puzzle! I loled at the ENT secret
Cute. Clever. Fun. <3

i sort of intuited the gimmick right away, but even when the puzzle was done i was still looking for some hidden meaning in the shaded squares, and finding none, which led me here. 

i am also always noticing odd quirks of words or word combinations, but i confess AOC and PTI had escaped my notice. most recently i was pondering how "ice"  can sound like "ights" leading to some very odd mistakes, e.g. my car needs new head lice; know your rice, Robin Hood men entice, etc
The shaded squares are unnecessary and caused the solver to look for something that wasn’t to be found.

'heart transplant's' is NOTHING compared to the wonderful clues and answers of the long crosses - THIS IS WHY WE DO CROSSWORDS.  absolutely hilarious ingenious fun witty and deeply thought out fun phrases based on a funny clue. if people were not giggling at how they worked you're missing the real point of the puzzle.  the meta conceit is there that's all - the clues are all classic and well loved.  what's not to LOVE? I loved it!
ELIE crossing JEMISIN and EID? Ouch!

The paper cut sayings made me feel wibbly-wobbly.

Just like the phrase, "sliding down the razor blade of life."
I did have to look up ECHIDNA to finish. New word for me.
It's a HINDU shindig, not a HINDI shindig. Hindu is the religion, Hindi is the language.
I loved the clue for “pointless!” I had to go to the notes to realize I’d spelled both Jemisin and Osiris wrong. But fun workout. 🙂

I wish I were an echidna.

Not the half-woman, half-snake monster (although that could be fun, too), but the cute little fella that looks like he was made in a Pixar studio.

Actually, thinking about it, I wish I were either of them.

Or at least a wombat.
Fun and not difficult but I never got the theme until after I solved the puzzle.

doubling down on how wonderful this puzzle is - this puzzle is a litmus test for people who are not satisfied by anything and those who truly understand how hilarious this puzzle is  -making the marquee answers be classic old school funny using similar letters. the mete theme is an afterthought and is fine why not? the heart and soul of the puzzle is the old school fun in those glorious crosses.  the fill is helpful for beginners and experts.  10 STARS!

I understood the gimmick early on, but I never understood how it translates to a “heart transplant”. Heart duplication, maybe? Heart mirror? But a transplant doesn’t leave you with two working hearts. (Yet. Come on, Science!)

Despite the theme confusion, I thought this was a pretty decent Sunday. On the easy side, but there were a few sticky sections. (AREEL / ETS, anyone?) And with cute fill like LOTSA FLOTSAM and PAPERCUT APERCU, who am I to complain?
Yes, Broken Earth trilogy! And loved the whimsy of the theme answers.

This was a strange solving experience for me.

I seemed to be getting just about everything, filling in block after block, but I ran into a single square that I wasn't quite sure of.  

So I do what I always to, and ignore it.  And it happened again, and again.

So I had all but about four separated single squares, and about a 50/50 guess for each of them--the D in DONNA, the I in LIS, the I in TIGER, and the T in ATE.

Made a best guess, and mirabile dictu, they were all right and no flyspecking, which would have been brutal.

Now that was an impressive theme - you might remember I'm in awe of a constructor's skill extremely rarely, and today was one of those days. That one of the themed entries referenced my beloved Star Trek was a nice bonus. I didn't even mind the slightly groany undertone of the theme, and that's saying something. Typically the merest hint of dad-jokery will put me off a grid.

The fill was mostly directly clued and easy to get. However, I needed to lookup the triple natick of the Berkeley university, TV network, and Cardinals legend (Richelieu wasn't it 🤣). Another natick was BE_ crossing DA_TON: I thought an L made sense there, but it turned out to be Y 🤷🏽. And one more natick - ESSE_ crossing AME_. After my recent visit to Germany I entered an N there. The problem is, AMEX is unknown over here, so the clue and entry of ESSE_'s cross were essentially useless to me. I've read about gerrymandering and I know about its history, but of course I didn't remember the first place it was applied.
So close to a personal best!

A comment on Will Shortz's anecdote in the first paragraph of wordplay:

The constructor, Michael Lieberman, appears to need constructing to deal with the stress of the baseball post season.

Ahem.

Mr. Lieberman is a Los Angeles Dodgers fan.  Let that sink in.

A *Dodgers* fan.

Mr. Lieberman, I doubt you'll get a lot of sympathy from other baseball fans here about your post-season trauma.  😀
Thank you, Michael Lieberman, that was great fun! For the second half, I had a smile on my face to the end.

Tough Sunday for me. 

Had to reveal papercutapercu. Didn't know apercu, had ace instead of ate, and had no idea who the sports legend was... I also have little patience for trial and error when I get to the end 🤣. 

So close, yet so far. Frustrating 😬😬😬
I loved this puzzle!!!

Finishing this splendid puzzle should have been as satisfying as staking out a certain bare chested President in Death Valley, pouring over buckets of gooey honey and waiting for a stream of journalist ants to arrive with microphones and notepads at the ready. Unfortunately, I had put a V in ADVG for advantage after a deuce point, so it wasn’t.
Fun and fast. I do think a better theme/title could have been found that wasn't so confusing/red herringish. But overall a great puzzle!

Great puzzle! Bizarre mix of very easy and very difficult clues. Just right for sharing with a loved one in Sunday morning, once you’ve filled in all the gimmes. 

As for the gimmick, I found that these are fairly easy to think up if you start with a word that you can add a letter to on each end, like LANE =>> P+LANE+T = PLANET

Fragrant waft from a hot beverage?
TEA STEAM

People who break the castling rules in chess?
ROOK CROOKS

Sixth sense on a scooter?
VESPA ESP

Roman galvanization?
LATIN PLATING

Any more (better!) suggestions? Happy Sunday everyone!

I got to KLINGONLINGO and was like eh, kinda obvious, this is going to be an average theme...but then EARCANALARCANA and PAPERCUTAPERCU came in with the folding chair and I have to say this is GRAND baby.. I love this kind of weirdness.  ggwp

Well that went quickly. Not surprised that it was my fastest Sunday ever. 

Maybe I would have enjoyed it more without the shaded squares. I got KLINGON LINGO much too easily, then all the themers were gimmes, or pretty close. If the squares hadn't been shaded, at least the break between the two words would have needed thought. 

The rest of the fill was mostly rote for me. Take 35D, like a blue moon or blue steak. Both halves of the clue were obvious, then they had to double up? I get that Sunday should be mid-week clues plus a bigger grid, but this one was just too easy to make it fun for me. Even our friend EEL had a boring clue. Where was "black and white sandwich cookie"?

I looked to see if there was some great Easter egg with the shaded letters. Nope, unless Knelodptfysgbgfm means something. Maybe the shape?? No again. I see no reason for the shaded squares except to make the puzzle easier for very new solvers. Maybe I would have appreciated that when I was a noob, but I'm more inclined to think I would have been more delighted by the discovery of the theme answers without the shaded training wheels.
doing the midi today, was confused when PAL wouldn't fit in for 15 across

50A? How about this one?

1A [How does California's *famousest* college rank this year?] SCALE

See, you've got "CAL" inside of "SCALE" ❤️❤️as in 

(from the world-renowned rankings by U.S. News and World Reports):
"University of California, Berkeley is a public institution that was founded in 1868. In the 2027 edition of Best Colleges, University of California, Berkeley is ranked No. 20 in National Universities. It's also ranked No. 1 in Top Public Schools."

Gotcha. Go Bears.
I am surely in a minority, but that was less a puzzle than it was 45 minutes of googling. My best to those who found it fun.
Fast and fun.
Fun gimmick, and "Get into, as a cab, say" takes the cake for the biggest groan-inducing-yet-appreciative-smile reaction from me in several weeks.

It’s been several months now and it’s still incredibly annoying that the hints/tips/comments page cannot open separately from the game itself. I’m sorry but I’m dumb and I often need a lot of help. It’s incredibly annoying having to click back and forth in order to see the hints then go back then click several buttons to see the hints again. 

This is not one of those things you can “get used to” especially when you need a lot of hints. it’s simply just appalling UX design. Please I beg you to revert back to what it’s used to be. I don’t care if this is due to whatever backend restructure. The front end is terrible! I know I’m not the only one as there had been many complains when this was first changed. I’ve tried to get used to it but it’s simply not possible. Please have pity on us dumb dumbs who need a lot of hints. I’ve found the only way is just to call up the answer key, which does open in a separate browser so I don’t have to click back and forth a million times. But this does take out a lot of joy from trying to do the puzzle.

Argh, this was so frustrating, a real game of two halves. I was flying along, loving it all, til the wheels fell off in the middle. Looking back I don’t really see what threw me so badly; yes, there were those small but pesky three letter entries that felt very American (REI, LOU, ETC, CAL,) but they held me up considerably longer than they should have. 
The theme was interesting. I agree with some here that not shading the letters would have been more interesting, especially as they don’t seem to have added anything to the grid in either a word, phrase or shape. Or did I miss something?

Still, any puzzle that notes the astounding Broken Earth trilogy is ok by me. I may have to go and re-read them, again, once I’ve finished my Bookclub homework (Violetta by Isabel Allende if you’re interested). 

Speaking of BOARS. Visiting friends in Toulouse, we witnessed a boar hunt in the neighbouring forest. Very French; a Deux Chevaux bristling with hunters. Next day we received a haunch after our friend was anointed with blood as it was his first hunt, to the horror of my then 9 yr old girl. We roasted it nice and slow. The best pork I’ve ever had in my life. With apologies to the non meat eaters. DD hasn’t touched pork since.
I wonder why the "heart-enclosing" boxes were shaded. Would it have made the puzzle more than just a little bit harder if that hadn't been done?
Outstanding.  Has everything a good puzzle needs.  Wit. Super clever Word play. Originality. Challenge.
Great puzzle. Only nit to pick is the use of (INK)PAD x2. Otherwise, well done and happy Sunday.

As for the theme, as it so often happens, it went from annoying--"look how much they muck things up trying to come up with a unique theme!"--to helpful, and thereby appreciated--"you know, it's a pretty clever theme, now that I think about it."
Loved it, except for one thing: The etymological relationship of SLOTH and "slow" is too recent and obvious, so (in my opinion) the latter should not be part of a clue for the former.
Fun, but too quick for a Sunday. I'm not done with my coffee yet.

And... that is just one truly amazing piece of construction to come up with all those answers that work both ways. Wow. Can't imagine what it took to come up with all of those answers.

Hope to read more Comments later.  Cranberries have hit the grocery store here, so I need to do a major batch of cranberry sauce.  (Some for us, and the rest for gifts.)  TTFN!

I enjoyed today's puzzle and the heart transplant linguistic trick.  BUT, Diwali, Holi, etc. are Hindu, not Hindi shindigs.  Characterizing them as "Hindi" omits non-Hindi Hindus, of whom there are over 500 million in India alone, for whom these are also delightful shindigs.

I got the theme through the APERCU APERCU doubling, because PAPERCUTAPERCU doesn't make sense.   I can't say I ATE this puzzle, however, because I didn't know that slang.   I was puzzled because AcE, my answer,  is not past tense.

Is there an email address anyone would recommend to send suggestions regarding the crossword puzzle? I have already tried using crosswordeditors@nytimes.com. I offered what I thought were helpful ideas to make the puzzle accessible to newcomers without alienating experienced solvers, but never got even the courtesy of a reply. I'm beginning to think they just don't care about us and expect us to just go into the archives. It's a win-win for them, because we're still spending time on the site, but they don't have to do anything for us. If that's what they're thinking, it's pretty disrespectful. The archive is all well and good, but I'd like to have some contemporary NYT puzzles to solve.
Fun puzzle

Very easy, very pleasant.  Of course I saw what was happening at KLINGON LINGO, a type of slang that's meaningless to me, but that revealed the theme.  Once I had gone past the slightly tricky EAR CANAL ARCANA and delightful PAPERCUT APERCU, I was home free -- with all the easy 2nd halves of the remaining themers guessed in advance.  

But because Michael Leiberman tends to clue with verve and panache, I never got bored with this.  And having an easy puzzle after the last two nightmarish days of all-Trivial Pursuit-all-the-time was a nice respite.  The headline is cute, btw.

I really liked the inclusion of shading for the theme answers. While I appreciate that some would have preferred a harder solve via s lack of shading, this one had way too much trivia (proper names) for me to solve without the help of shading. KLINGON LINGO gave me the theme and was fun. I also enjoyed all the misdirects, like UNCORK for getting into a cab. Thank you. Fun.
This keeps happening...Im working the puzzle, today I was over half done, and I navigate away. When I return to the puzzle all my recent entries are gone. Whats going on? This never used to happen.
Solved this one almost 10 minutes faster than my average and set a new PR!

Before he got his own animated show, Daniel TIGER was a hand puppet who had chats with Mr. Rogers. It took me while to make that connection when I started seeing the related products in the A to Z warehouse.

APERCU is one of those words I've read in the evening and resolved to look up in the morning...but never remembered.

Felicitations to all.

I was blasting through this one and loving it until I hit the crossings of JEMISIN/ELIE, PEI/ETE, and AREEL/EFTS/I'M ALONE.

I'm got lost on IMA_ONE for "out of date" -- without the L I kept thinking about whether "date" was a fruit, expiration deadline, timeline (like you've been teleported to prehistoric times), age group, or romantic partner. I'm guessing it's like if you're asking for a table for one? Or like if you're at a party surrounded by others outside your age group? I'm stumped.

Lovely theme, but I didn't love those crossers which did me in. PEI/ETE alone would've blocked me without running the alphabet or at least the vowels. No gold star for me today.
I probably would have set my Sunday best time were it not for the bandage on my right index fingertip.

A fun puzzle today!

I knew this would be fun when I saw the name, and I was right. Some of these answers just made me laugh. Also, I once saw Lou Brock play in St. Louis. Bob Gibson too. And that was a lot of fun too.
Fun puzzle! SE corner was rough with the nouns and slang, but not prohibitive. Great Sunday!!
Was hoping the shaded letters would provide a reveal, but still a fun, well-constructed puzzle.

Fun puzzle! Always love a mention of "Mr. Blue Sky," and the theme answers are pretty delightful to read aloud. But I think my favorite part is that the constructor shares a last name with our cardiologist, specifically the one who has seen my mom through a lot of scary health events, so solving his heart puzzle really made me smile. 

Happy Sunday to you all!
98 Across: The answer Hindi shindig is nonsensical and should have been caught in editing. Hindi is a language. The holidays are Hindu.
I know I have everything correct and keep getting the “almost there” note… I even overlaid it on the answer key to make sure… this is driving me nuts! Anyone else?

I loved the theme answers. Each one delightful. Klingon Lingo and Last in Blasting, Lotsa flotsam! And I'm sure I am not the only one who gets a kick every time a "cab" clue refers to wine and not a taxi! And who hasn't overdid Verdi on a cold winter morning?! Clever, but very easy for me.
I can't be the only one who cringed at the triumphal arch. Can I? It ain't easy living in our nation's capitol these days.

Completely charming puzzle. I messed myself up a little putting in Jaques Brel the singer/actor instead of Jacques the filmmaker. 

Thought I had the theme quickly, but really just got it in stages. 

1. Early, saw that removing the gray letters resulted in reduplication.
2. Late, saw that removing those squares always left actual words. 
3. After reading the column, learned that both shaded squares were always within the same word.

I had completely missed the containment part of the theme. Even so, just using the reduplicative aspect let me fill in most of my gaps. And each theme reveal was delightful.
Can someone explain how the shaded squares relate to "heart transplant". I don't see a heart.
Sensational puzzle and validating community that struggled with the same challenges. A very satisfying Sunday crossword puzzle experience!
Jacques TATI--"Mr. Hulot's Holiday" a classic https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ro1OBd_WruA

A fun puzzle, and I really enjoyed the AHA moment when the theme fell into place. And APERCU was a new one on me, I was very doubtful of its answer ending in a U until the theme forced it into place and I looked it up afterwards.

A really fun and approachable puzzle!
I often marvel at the ingenuity of the constructors and especially with one like this.
My favorite was LOTSAfLOTSAm.  I find it hard to believe that someone could think of this, but the constructor did.
That brings up a point I have often thought about recently in light of events we constantly read about.  I am aware that constructors use software to help in their efforts, but is the day coming when AI will be the common constructor?  Are puzzles we see constructed by AI now?

Someone yesterday suggested the October 10, 2013 Saturday puzzle. Foolishly, I tried it. I mean, I have worked other puzzles in the archive from way back and this one was from the Shortz era, after all.

Wowza. I spent almost two hours on it but this is deceptive because at one point I could not see any way to forge ahead. None. Later I decided to try once more before abandoning. I took out a whole bunch of stuff and tried some unlikely possibilities, one of which turned out to be right.

In the end, I used online dictionaries to check my spelling for the Macedonian capital (correct) and the Moravian city (incorrect, I had a city in Bosnia instead). But it turned out my real mistake was in how I spelled the French phrase, the only second language I ever studied. That did leave a more palatable answer for "Abandon one's efforts," which I had filled with something decidedly unpalatable. 

Is it just because I found it so difficult that it seemed less humor-filled than most present day Shortz edits? And before anyone suggests this, the trivia was not the difficulty. There was nothing I had not heard of before, once I filled it in.

Wowza wowza.
A find puzzle, I guess but I spent FAR too much time trying to make the words "LITTORAL" and "LITTER" somehow work for the answer to 120 Across.

Would have expected the NY Times to have caught the very annoying mistake of confounding a language (Hindi) with a religion (Hindu). To put it in context, Hindi is the mother tongue of 18% of Indians. Around 70% of Indians are Hindus. It’s like Taylor mentioned in his comment, “It’s like describing Christmas as a Spanish celebration.”
A personal Natick at Queen BEY crossing the DAYTON Flyers did not stop me from getting a new Sunday best.
These kind of word puzzles remind me of my own train of thought when I am hiking or walking the dog alone.  The cleverness is fun and I didn’t want the journey to end.

Count me among those who thinks Hindi shindig doesn't make sense. Hindi is just a language, not a religion or culture, and the words themselves come from Sanskrit. 

I see that some people have made the argument that it works because people who celebrate speak Hindi. A) Not everyone does, and B) many celebrants speak English, but I'm guessing no one would call Diwali or Holi an English shindig.
Fun puzzle. But I still don't get the heart transplants theme. Please explain.

Nothing 'snappy' about this puzzle.  I come here about once a year to comment, really good, or really bad.  This is that day.  This is recycled Monday fill, dressed up as a Sunday puzzle.  I expect more from the NYT team.  And the answer at 98 Across - isn't this why xword editors exist?

Meh. Still don't get and don't care to get the theme, even after reading the article, which I normally don't do. This wordplay was cute but did not find this cohesive and some of the cluing was a tad awkward or inaccurate in order to construct the puzzle to make the theme. Same with some obscure trivia, at least for me. I'm glad I ignored the gray squares from the get go. That said, who doesn't like a puzzle that has sloths and echidnas in it.

Fun puzzle, and getting the theme helped me fill in some squares, which is always enjoyable.

Apercu scared me, but i am fairly ignorant and knew that it could be a word that I had never seen before.

And along the lines of ignorance is bliss, Hindi didn't bother me at all.

51:25 unaided. A nice bit of entertainment.
Exceptionally clever!

Hmmmm....clever theme, but I am a bit confused about the heart transplant bit? Is it because the "heart" of the word(s) are to be found as the final word of the clue's answer? If so, wouldn't it be SHINDIG HINDI?
I had GUM for 36D and was confused when I realized it had to start with a C.

If my engine was clunking as hard as some of those puns, I'd sacrifice a lawyer or two to the god of warranties. Why is offering a handful of ponderously-worded, low-effort clues once or twice a week considered a better option by the Times than publishing a proper cryptic edited by someone with less sympathy for the least-able solvers?
Enjoyable puzzle. Re 69A, I have read and very highly recommend the Broken Earth trilogy by N.K. JEMISIN.

Certain words are classic crosswordese, meaning that you will start to recognize them by their clues immediately and have the gimme-est of gimmes.  EFT(S) is one of those words.

In the plural, it has appeared 209 times, while the singular has appeared 197 times (although a handful recently have been clued to Electronic Funds Transfers).  Whenever you see something about young newts, salamanders, amphibians, etc., it's going to be EFT(S).  Put it in your pocket for next time.

Interestingly, NEWT and EFT are basically the same word.  NEWT developed by rebracketing, a linguistic process where a letter moves from one word in a phrase to the adjacent one; in this case, "an eft" became "a neft," and then underwent a slight transformation to "a newt."  You find this phenomenon in "apron," which was once "napron," and "orange" ("norange").

In Poland we might speak of a street as it being the main one in town, but no street is actually officially called that. Historically, the main streets of Polish settlements were often named after the largest nearby town or city. Thus, for example, many a Mazovian main street is "ulica Warszawska" (Mazowsze is Warsaw's region; "warszawska" is the feminine form of Warsaw used as an adjective - and we're using the feminine form here since "ulica", "street", is a feminine noun in our gendered language). @Nancy J. I have mixed feelings about this. On one hand I deeply appreciate any ideas that will help the puzzles retain their original appeal. On the surface, a training-wheel clue set and perhaps optional overlays (shaded boxes etc) would do what you say: keep the puzzles puzzling for those who like the challenge, and help new solvers get to grips with the way the puzzles work. On the other hand, the NYT crossword can only hold its status as a prestige puzzle if it accepts with its whole heart that it is simply not for everyone.

It’s ok that new solvers cannot, for example, easily zip through Saturdays. I remember the days of my daughter’s gymnastics lessons when I’d drop her off and then go to a coffee shop and usually take that full 45 minutes trying to untangle the puzzle, often with a lot of lookups. Now I can’t remember the last time I looked anything up, and Saturdays take the time I used to allocate to a good Wednesday.

This is all to say: if something is worth doing—and I think the classic NYT crossword is worth doing—it’s worth doing properly, with effort. If someone wants to be the kind of person who solves this crossword every day, it’s up to them to become that kind of person through developing their skill. It’s not up to the puzzles themselves to change in any way at all. 

Changing the puzzles in the ways you suggest would, in my opinion, ultimately devalue them. But maybe no more than they’re already being devalued. It’s a tricky one.
